body: The railings outside a small church hall are being repainted on the first warm weekend of the year, and a girl of about nine is holding the tin because she has been told to be useful and this is the useful thing. The door behind her father is propped open with a fire extinguisher. Inside, a deacon is going over a chant for the morning, unaccompanied, no chords under it, the line bending in places a piano could not follow. She asks what language that is. Her father says he thinks it is the old one. He has been hearing it since he was her age and it has never once occurred to him to ask.

The old one has a name, and the name is the whole point. What the deacon was practising was not a stylistic decision and it was not heritage kept up for the grandparents. It was a survival — something that came east and stayed east, and was never routed through anywhere else on its way in.

The standard mental map has the faith beginning in Jerusalem, moving west into Europe, maturing there for a millennium and a half, and then being carried outward to everybody else in the modern period.

That map is not false so much as one-directional. It records a real journey and quietly omits the other one. The faith moved east at the same time as it moved west, along the roads that carried everything else — the trade routes up through Persia, across Central Asia and on into China. The churches on those roads were not outposts of anybody. They had their own patriarch, their own schools of theology, their own liturgical language, and they went where the merchants went. In Xi’an there is a stone stele, cut in the Tang period and still standing, which records a Christian mission received at the imperial court. Somebody was there, and somebody thought it worth cutting into rock.

The dial this article sits on runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 40 are international — one permanent frequency per language, hosted in that language rather than dubbed into it afterwards.

Assigning frequencies that way costs something, and the cost is the point. A number given to a language cannot later be handed to a bigger audience, and several of those languages will never attract an advertiser. The expensive form of respect is to give a church a frequency of its own and keep it there. The cheap form is a world hour on somebody else’s station, and it has been tried before: the missionaries who arrived in Kerala met congregations whose liturgy was older than their own countries’ conversion, and treated them as a field to be worked.

That encounter keeps happening in smaller ways, and the reason is not malice. It is a curriculum. Church history as it is usually taught runs from Jerusalem to Antioch to Rome to Wittenberg to Aldersgate, and a student can complete the whole of it without learning that there was a patriarch in Baghdad corresponding with bishops in India. The art does the same work. Centuries of paintings put the events in a northern light, on northern faces, and a picture teaches faster than a paragraph. Nobody set out to erase a direction. It fell off the edge of the frame, and the frame got hung in every hall.

The band is partitioned the way a broadcast band is — a five-fold band for the ministry stations, a multilanguage band for the nations, a mainstream band for the always-on formats. The international stations sit together in a block, grouped by region, so the neighbours of a frequency tell you something about it before you have heard a note. Learn roughly where the block begins and you can move around inside it without looking anything up, which is the skill an actual dial teaches and a search field never does.
Which raises a question a station in a language has to answer before it broadcasts anything. Who is it for?

The obvious answer is that it is for reaching people, and there is nothing wrong with that answer as far as it goes. Broadcasting has been used for outreach for as long as there has been broadcasting, and a great deal of good has come of it. But an outreach frequency has a shape. It assumes the listener is outside and must be brought in, it explains what the listener already knows, and it is pitched throughout to somebody who has not heard. Point that shape at a community that has held the faith longer than the broadcaster’s own country has, and every hour of it is quietly insulting.
You cannot reach a church that got there before you.

A man in his sixties is sitting in the cab of a parked van on an industrial estate outside Coventry with twenty minutes of his break left and a foil tray of rice going cold on the passenger seat. He is from Thrissur and has been in England thirty-one years. The radio in the cab only gets the local station, so he puts something on through his phone instead, and what comes out is a Chinese setting of a psalm — women’s voices, a melody that goes somewhere he was not expecting, no drums at all. He listens to the whole of it with the tray untouched. Then he texts his son, who is at university in Leeds and does not go to anything, to say there were Christians in China before there were Christians in England. His son sends back a question mark. He does not answer, because the next song has started.
Nothing in that van required anybody to have been persuaded of anything. A fact he had known his whole life came at him from an unexpected direction, in a language he does not speak, and landed.

It is only honest to say what this argument cannot do. Most of that eastern church is gone. The roads closed, the empires turned over, communities were pressed and taxed and scattered, and much of what was sung along those routes was never written down and is not recoverable by anybody now. You cannot tune to the seventh century. A frequency can carry a living church in a living language; it cannot carry back what was lost, and it would be a cheat to imply otherwise.

But the loss is an argument for broadcasting, not against it. Everything that did survive survived because somebody kept doing it out loud, in front of children who were not paying attention, in rooms where nothing important appeared to be happening. That is the only mechanism there has ever been. A liturgy still sung on a Sunday morning in Kerala is not a museum piece; it is the same act of maintenance that carried it from one century to the next, continued by other means.

So the point is not that the eastern church is a footnote to the western one. The point is that there was never a single direction of travel, and a listener whose family has been Christian in Asia for longer than anybody can count is not receiving something. They are holding something. That is the difference between being told your faith is an import and knowing it is an inheritance, and it is no small difference to grow up on one side of.
All of which is history until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, of which 40 carry a frequency now and more are assigned and still in build.

If you want somewhere to start after reading this, start at HM 334.40 — Asia Inspire, the Chinese-language station. Start there whether or not you speak a word of it, and start there precisely because of what this article has been arguing. Chinese-language Christianity is filed in the Western mind under the nineteenth century, as though it began with a mission society and a steamer, and that stone in Xi’an has been standing the whole time saying otherwise. Put the station on and you are not listening to the results of an outreach campaign. You are listening to a church singing in a language that had a Christian vocabulary in it while a good deal of Europe was still being argued into the faith one kingdom at a time.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a correction. You are not being asked to relearn church history this afternoon, and you do not need a settled view on any of it in order to press play. Put HM 334.40 on while you are doing something else and let it run for an hour. You will not understand the words. You will understand perfectly well that nobody in the recording is explaining themselves to you, and that is the whole of what this article has been trying to say, arriving with no argument attached.
